title: From Sensor Readings to Maintenance Decisions: A Failure-Mode-Based Health, Confidence, and Risk Framework for Utility Switchgear
content: Switchgear rarely fails because of age alone. It fails when a joint heats up, insulation starts to discharge, a mechanism sticks after months of standing idle, or a heater quietly stops working. Fixed-interval maintenance catches some of these problems, but it also takes healthy equipment out of service and can miss defects that develop between visits. This paper reviews and extends a recent utility framework by Muthu et al. for condition-based management of medium- and high-voltage switchgear. We describe the asset by subsystem, link each credible failure mode to the measurements that can reveal it, and outline the main monitoring methods. These include thermal sensing, partial discharge, contact resistance, timing and travel, coil and motor current, vibration, gas condition, and environmental and auxiliary supervision. We then explain the proposed scoring scheme. It keeps four quantities apart: condition, confidence in the data, probability of failure, and consequence. A worst-mode rule stops one serious defect from being averaged away. We add a worked numerical example for a 15 kV fleet of three breakers. With a worst-mode weight of 0.8, a hot primary contact pulls the health index from 80 to 56 instead of hiding behind healthy subsystems. A breaker with a failed mechanism monitor scores 92 on health but only 57 on confidence, which flags it for inspection. Our analysis also exposes two gaps in the method. First, a lone low-quality reading can set a failure-mode score on its own, so an explicit “unknown” threshold is needed. Second, the thermal indicator is biased at light load when temperature rise does not scale exactly with the square of current.
